newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's cabinet grapples with strike crisis.
newsitem.headline: Spain's cabinet grapples with strike crisis.

text.p: Spain's government, grappling with a burgeoning economic crisis caused by a nine-day-old truckers strike, was on Friday considering a demand that it reduce diesel prices.
But such a step was not expected to end the standoff.
The agriculture sector has lost some 20 billion pesetas ($140 million) so far with milk, meat and vegetables worst hit, the farmer's cooperative CCAE estimated on Friday.
The Economy Ministry has warned a continuation of the strike would push fish, fruit and vegetable prices strongly higher.
Meanwhile, the strike looked set to broaden, with taxi unions calling on members to join it on Monday.
Striking truckers have choked roads in northern Spain, cut off supplies to many areas and forced factories to shut.
By Friday, the chaos was spreading south.
In a copycat action to the French truckers strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of the sector.
They want the retirement age lowered to 60 years from 65 and are pushing for diesel subsides, a revision of tariffs and recognition of occupational illnesses.
Unions said the government may approve one of their demands to cut diesel prices at their weekly cabinet meeting.
But service stations warned they too would take action if such a measure were approved.
"This would mean the total ruin of 80 percent of service stations," said the Spanish Confederation of Service Stations.
The government criticised leading union Fedatrans, which initially called the strike, for boycotting talks.
Representatives from the development, labour, economy and industry ministries met a number of transport associations on Thursday but Fedatrans refused to join them.

"An end to the strike will only be achieved if the Cabinet calls an urgent meeting to create an interministerial commission with powers to coordinate restructuring of the sector," Fedatrans said in a statement.
Meanwhile thousands of trucks lined the hard shoulders of main roads and pickets initimidated any drivers who dared to pass.
With truckers blockading border crossings, hundreds of foreign drivers also found themselves caught up in the jam.
More than a thousand Portuguese trucks were stranded at the border at Vilar Formoso and Caia, and hundreds of French trucks were also stuck at Behovia-Irun, local media said..
French truckers said Spanish pickets had attacked them.

The French Road Haulage Federation said the violence was probably in retaliation for the death of a Spanish picket run over on Thursday by a French truck driver. French authorities have barred trucks from entering northwestern Spain.
The Interior Ministry ordered security forces to guarantee essential supplies to towns and free up blocked roads, but food supplies remained short in many towns.
Companies complained that getting supplies through to their factories was proving too dangerous and many were forced to shut down production, with car manufacturers were worst hit.
German carmaker Mercedes Benz said its supplies had been disrupted on Thursday as pickets dropped rocks from bridges on their trucks, despite a police escort.
British supermarket chain Tesco said its trucks were also damaged and a driver sent to hospital after pickets dropped concrete from a motorway bridge.
Some companies resorted to air-lifting supplies.
Portugal's Ford, Volkswagen and AutoEuropa car manufacturers ordered special flights, while Tesco said it would fly food into Britain.
($ = 143.0 Spanish Pesetas)
